questions.question: A loss X takes values zero and one half with positive probability. The count PGF is the power series $G_N(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}(N=k)z^k$ for a non-negative integer-valued N. Why does X not satisfy this stated count domain?
options: A count PGF requires every possible value to be strictly positive.
Two possible values are insufficient for a count PGF.
One of its possible values is not an integer.
Unequal probabilities prevent a count PGF.

questions.question: A non-negative integer count N has PGF $G_N(z)=\mathbb{E}[z^N]$, using $z^0=1$ even at zero. What does evaluating at $z=0$ retain?
options: $\mathbb{P}(N=0)$.
$\mathbb{P}(N>0)$.
$\mathbb{E}[N]$.
$0$ regardless of the zero-count probability.

questions.question: A non-negative integer count N has an infinite mean. For real $0\le z\le1$, what does the bound $0\le z^N\le1$ establish about its PGF $G_N(z)=\mathbb{E}[z^N]$?
options: It diverges throughout this interval because the mean is infinite.
It is finite only at zero because positive z weights large counts.
It is finite only at one because the probabilities sum to one.
It is finite throughout this interval despite the infinite mean.

questions.question: Two non-negative integer counts X and Y have PGFs with identical coefficients of every power of z. What information does this equality identify?
options: Their realised counts must be identical in every outcome.
Their marginal count distributions are identical.
Their joint distribution must be independent.
Their two means determine all coefficients.

questions.question: Non-negative integer counts X and Y are allowed to be dependent. A proposed argument replaces $\mathbb{E}[z^{X+Y}]$ by $\mathbb{E}[z^X]\mathbb{E}[z^Y]$ for every $0<z<1$. Which missing premise is needed for the usual product-PGF theorem?
options: Independence of X and Y.
Equality of their two means.
Equality of their two PGFs.
Finiteness of their realised sum.

questions.question: A count has polynomial PGF $G(z)=0.2+0.3z+0.5z^2$. Its second derivative at zero is one. Using coefficient recovery, what is the probability of count two?
A count N equals zero with probability 0.4 and two with probability 0.6. What is its PGF value $G_N(1/2)=\mathbb{E}[(1/2)^N]$?
A non-negative integer count N has PGF $G_N(z)=0.3+0.7z$. A second count is the certain shift K=N+1. Which expression is $G_K(z)$?
Independent counts X,Y have PGFs $G_X(z)=0.8+0.2z$ and $G_Y(z)=0.5+0.5z$. What is $\mathbb{P}(X+Y=1)$ from their product PGF?

A nonnegative integer count has PGF G with left derivatives $G'(1-)=0.3$ and $G''(1-)=0$. The second derivative averages $N(N-1)$. Which PGF is consistent with both derivatives and probability normalisation?
A non-negative integer count N has PGF $G_N(z)=\mathbb{E}[z^N]$. Let $p_e$ and $p_o$ be its probabilities of an even and an odd count. What does $G_N(-1)$ equal?
options: $p_e+p_o$.
$p_o-p_e$.
$p_e-p_o$.

questions.question: A non-negative integer count N has PGF $G_N$ with $G_N(0)=1$. What stronger conclusion follows from probability normalisation?
options: N has mean one whenever its mean is finite.
Every positive count has the same probability.
N can give count two positive mass while keeping this zero coefficient.
N is zero with probability one.

questions.question: A count N has masses $\mathbb{P}(N=k)=2^{-(k+1)}$ for $k=0,1,\ldots$. Its PGF is finite on the unit interval. What happens at argument z=2?
options: It equals one because the masses sum to one.
It equals two because the argument is two.
It equals one half because only the constant term survives.
It diverges because every series term is one half.

questions.question: A non-negative integer count has exponential transform $M_N(t)=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{tN}]$ finite exactly when $t<\log 2$. For positive z, where is $G_N(z)=M_N(\log z)$ finite?
A count N has finite PGF derivatives $G_N'(1)=2$ and $G_N''(1)=6$. What is its raw second moment $\mathbb{E}[N^2]$?
A proposed count transform is $H(z)=0.6-0.1z+0.5z^2$, so $H(1)=1$. Is H a PGF of a non-negative integer count?
options: Yes; the value one at z=1 is sufficient.
Yes; the positive constant and highest coefficient dominate.
No; the coefficient of z is a negative probability.
No; a count PGF must have infinitely many nonzero coefficients.

questions.question: Two count laws have PGFs $G_X(z)=1/2+z^2/2$ and $G_Y(z)=1/3+z/2+z^3/6$. Both have first and second derivatives at one equal to one. Does agreement of these two factorial moments identify their distributions?
options: Yes; the first two derivatives identify every count probability.
No; their probabilities at zero differ despite the matching moments.
Yes; a factorial second moment equal to the squared mean certifies a Poisson law.
No; the polynomials fail probability normalisation.

questions.question: Counts X,Y take values 0,1,2 with joint masses, with rows X=0,1,2 and columns Y=0,1,2, $(1,2,0)/9$, $(0,1,2)/9$, $(2,0,1)/9$. Both marginal PGFs are $(1+z+z^2)/3$, and diagonal sums give $G_{X+Y}(z)=(1+2z+3z^2+2z^3+z^4)/9=G_X(z)G_Y(z)$. Does this product equality establish independence?
options: Yes; equality of the sum PGF and the product is sufficient.
Yes; uniform marginal probabilities force uniform joint probabilities.
No; the diagonal masses fail to sum to one.
No; the joint mass at (0,1) is 2/9 rather than 1/9.

questions.question: A count has PGF $G(z)=0.2+az+bz^2+0.1z^3$, with unknown non-negative coefficients a,b. Its mean is 1.3. Which pair meets both probability normalisation and the derivative mean condition?

Count X is certainly one. Count Y is zero with probability 0.6 and three with probability 0.4. A proposed inference says $G_X(1/2)<G_Y(1/2)$ implies $\mathbb{E}[X]>\mathbb{E}[Y]$. Which evaluation tests this inference?
options: $0.5>0.05$, so its premise fails.
